title: The whole phase is one chain
summary: The language of money is not eight separate topics; it is one chain from rent to value, from cost to margin, from leverage to return, and from profit to cash and tax. This checkpoint lesson walks the chain once on a single hypothetical project and marks the three links where developers most often break it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the last eight weeks were one chain, not eight topics. Rent becomes net operating income, income becomes value, value less cost becomes margin, leverage turns margin into return, and timing and tax decide how much of that return reaches you as cash. Every serious mistake in development is a broken link somewhere on that chain.

Recall

Q. From last week: what is the output of reverse engineering a price?

A. A list headed "What must be true," each line graded by its evidence, with the answer given as a range.

Q. From the valuation week: where does each of the three approaches bend?

A. The income approach bends at the cap rate and at how honestly NOI was normalised; the sales comparison approach at the adjustments; the cost approach at depreciation.

Q. From the value week: what is yield on cost?

A. Stabilised net operating income divided by total project cost, the return the finished building earns on what it cost to create.

Why this matters

A checkpoint is where recognition becomes recall. You have met every idea in this phase once. In a meeting you will need them together, in order, and fast: a lender will ask about your spread, then your contingency, then your interest reserve, then your exit cap rate, in under a minute. If you hold the chain as one picture, each answer leads to the next. If you hold eight separate lessons, you will answer each question well and still lose the room.

The chain, walked once

One hypothetical project, round numbers throughout. Eighty apartments, 4,800 square metres rentable.

Link one: rent to NOI. Potential gross rent of $1,728,000, less 5 percent vacancy, is $1,641,600 of effective gross income. Less 30 percent operating expenses, net operating income (NOI) is about $1,150,000. This is the second pro forma week: income is only as good as its vacancy, expense and lease-up assumptions.

Link two: NOI to value. At a 5 percent cap rate the finished building is worth about $23,000,000. This is the valuation week: the cap rate is an opinion drawn from a handful of sales, and half a point moves value by about 10 percent.

Link three: value against cost. Total cost, from the first pro forma week, is land $1,500,000, hard costs $15,000,000, soft costs $2,700,000 and finance costs $1,400,000, about $20,600,000. Yield on cost is $1,150,000 divided by $20,600,000, about 5.6 percent. The development spread is 5.6 less 5.0, about 60 basis points. That is thin, and the value week told you why it matters: the spread is your pay for taking development risk.

Link four: margin to return. Profit is $23,000,000 less $20,600,000, or $2,400,000, about 12 percent on cost. With a 65 percent loan, equity is about $7,210,000. The equity gets back $7,210,000 plus $2,400,000, a multiple of about 1.33. Over three years the rough internal rate of return (IRR) is about 10 percent. This is the returns week: leverage magnifies both ways, and IRR must be read beside the multiple.

Link five: return to cash and tax. The accounting weeks taught that profit and cash run on different clocks. Most of the cash goes out in years one and two and comes back in year three; interest during construction is capitalised into cost rather than paid from income. Then tax takes its share at the entity and personal level, the after-tax leakage from the returns week. The return you can spend is smaller and later than the return on the pro forma.

Say that out loud now.

The three links that break most often

The cap rate at exit. Value at link two is set years before the building is finished. Rerun the project with a 5.5 percent exit cap rate: value falls to about $20,900,000, which is barely above the $20,600,000 cost. Profit falls from $2,400,000 to about $300,000. Half a point of cap rate removed seven eighths of the profit. Because profit is a small number left over between two large ones, it moves far more than either.

Cost against estimate class. The first pro forma week taught that an early estimate is a range, not a number. If the hard cost of $15,000,000 is an early-class estimate with a plausible range of 20 percent either way, the $3,000,000 upper half of that range is larger than the entire profit. A contingency that does not reflect the estimate class is decoration.

Cash before profit. A project can show a profit and still run out of money in month 14, because draws lag work, retainage is held back and lease-up starts late. The statements weeks taught that cash is a timetable. The lender's interest reserve and your own liquidity floor are what keep the timetable from killing the profit.

Worked example two: the one link you control

Of everything on the chain, the land price is the input you negotiate directly. Run the same project with land at $700,000 instead of $1,500,000. Total cost falls to about $19,800,000. Yield on cost rises to about 5.8 percent, so the spread widens to about 80 basis points. Profit becomes $3,200,000, about 16 percent on cost. Equity at 35 percent of cost is about $6,930,000, the multiple about 1.46, and the rough three-year IRR about 13 percent. Now stress it at the 5.5 percent exit cap rate: profit falls to about $1,100,000 rather than to $300,000. The building, the rents and the costs are identical. Only the land price changed, and it decided whether a bad exit was survivable. That is why the checkpoint keeps returning to land: it is the residual, and it is where your discipline shows up as money.

How the best do it

Well-run institutional developers typically review every project on a single page that follows this exact chain, in this order: income, value, cost, spread, return, cash, and a short sensitivity table for exit cap rate, rent and hard cost. The discipline is not the complexity of the model; it is that every investment committee sees the same seven lines in the same order, so a weak link is visible at a glance and nobody can lead with the return while hiding the spread. A small developer can copy that page in an afternoon and use it for every deal, including the ones he rejects.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leading with the end of the chain. Investors ask for the IRR first, and the temptation is to give it. But IRR is the most derived number in the chain: it inherits every assumption above it. The control is to present in chain order, rent and NOI first, spread before return, and to put the exit cap rate sensitivity beside the headline return every time.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a thin spread as acceptable because the IRR looks fine. In the example, a 60 basis point spread still produced a 10 percent IRR on paper. But that IRR came almost entirely from leverage, and half a point of cap rate wiped out most of the profit. A thin spread with a healthy-looking IRR is a warning, not a reassurance.

Callback

In week 1 Remi described the developer's job as managing value levers through go/no-go gates. This chain is what each gate is checking. At the land gate you are testing links one to three with rough numbers. At the financing gate you are testing link four. At the construction gate you are testing link five, because that is where the cash runs out. The gates and the chain are the same idea seen from two sides.

Recap

Rent to NOI, NOI to value, value against cost, margin to return, return to cash and tax. The links that break most often are the exit cap rate, the estimate class behind the cost and the timing of cash. Present in chain order, and never let the return hide the spread.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on a contractor that reported profits while its cash ran out.
checklist: Write the five links from memory: rent to NOI, NOI to value, value against cost, margin to return, return to cash and tax.
Calculate the development spread before the IRR on every deal.
Rerun value at an exit cap rate half a point worse.
Check that contingency matches the estimate class of the cost.
Build a monthly cash timetable, not only an annual profit figure.
Present every deal in chain order on one page.
Treat a thin spread with a healthy IRR as a warning.
head: Field checklist
speak: The language of money is one chain. Rent, less vacancy and expenses, becomes net operating income. NOI divided by the cap rate becomes value. Value against total cost gives yield on cost and the development spread. Leverage turns the margin into a levered return. And timing and tax decide how much of that return reaches me as cash. On a hypothetical 80-unit building, NOI of 1.15 million at a 5 percent cap is about 23 million of value against 20.6 million of cost: a 60 basis point spread and a 2.4 million profit. Move the exit cap rate to 5.5 and the profit falls to about 300,000. That is the first weak link. The second is cost against estimate class, and the third is cash timing. So I present every deal in chain order, spread before return, with the cap rate sensitivity beside the headline IRR.
terms: Development spread — yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin paid for taking development risk.
Exit cap rate — the cap rate assumed when the finished building is valued or sold, often years after the decision to build.
Capitalised interest — interest during construction added to project cost rather than paid from income.

hostile.q: Your deal shows a 10 percent IRR. Why are you telling me about a 60 basis point spread instead?
hostile.a: Because the IRR is the most derived number on the page and the spread is the honest one. With a 60 basis point spread, a half-point rise in the exit cap rate cuts our profit from about 2.4 million to about 300,000, and the IRR comes almost entirely from leverage. I would not fund this at today's land price. At a lower price, or with signed rents that lift NOI, the spread widens and I will bring it back.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: Carillion 2018: profit on paper, no cash in the bank
summary: Carillion, a large British construction and services contractor, reported profits on long contracts while its cash position weakened, and it went into liquidation in January 2018. The case gathers the hardest ideas of this phase: profit versus cash, estimates inside accounts, and incentives that reward the reported number. It ends with Rule 18 on reconciling profit to cash.
rule: Rule 18: Every month I reconcile the profit a project, partner or contractor reports to the cash actually collected and paid; if the gap widens two months running, I stop advancing money until the cash explains the profit.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a company can report a profit every year and still run out of cash, because profit on a long construction contract is an estimate and cash is not. Carillion is the clearest large example. Cole sits beside me today, because the warning signs were in the accounts for anyone who reconciled the two.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what are the five links of the money chain?

A. Rent to net operating income, income to value, value against cost, margin to return, and return to cash and tax.

Q. From the owner accounting week: what is work in progress?

A. The cost of work done that has not yet been billed or completed, carried on the balance sheet until it becomes a finished asset or a sale. It depends on estimates of how far along the work is.

Q. From the statements week: why can a profitable project run short of cash?

A. Because profit records revenue and expense when earned or incurred, while cash moves on its own timetable: draws, deposits, retainage and lender holdbacks.

Why this matters

You will hire contractors whose balance sheets you cannot see in detail, and you will report to lenders and partners on projects whose profit is partly an estimate. Carillion shows both sides: the contractor that looked sound until the day it was not, and the reporting method that allowed the gap between profit and cash to grow quietly. The facts below come from public reporting and parliamentary material; verify the specifics against primary sources before you cite them.

Step 1: Timeline

Carillion was a large British company that built infrastructure and buildings and provided facilities services, much of it for government. Through the mid-2010s it won large, long contracts, including hospital projects and a major road scheme in Scotland, and continued to pay dividends. In July 2017 it issued a profit warning, announcing a large write-down on contract values, and its chief executive left. Further warnings followed in the autumn. Talks with lenders and government failed, and on 15 January 2018 the company entered compulsory liquidation. Two parliamentary committees issued a joint report later that year that was sharply critical of the board, and the audit later became the subject of regulatory action.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions stand out. First, bidding for large, complex contracts at thin margins, often with fixed prices that placed cost risk on the contractor. Second, recognising profit on those contracts using optimistic estimates of their final outcome, including the expectation of recovering money through claims and variations not yet agreed. Third, continuing to pay dividends and fund a growing pension deficit while cash generation was weak, and supporting cash by stretching payments to suppliers.

Step 3: Assumptions

On a long construction contract, accounting standards commonly allow revenue and profit to be recognised as the work progresses, based on the expected final result. That requires estimates: total cost to complete, final contract value and the likely outcome of claims. Carillion's reported margins assumed those estimates would come good. When the company reassessed them in 2017, the write-down showed that earlier reported profit had depended on outcomes that did not arrive. The cash never had: it was waiting on certification, disputes and claims.

Step 4: Incentives

Cole's view from the auditor's chair. Pay and bonuses tied to reported profit reward optimistic contract estimates. Dividends paid out of reported profit reward the same thing. Suppliers on long payment terms fund the contractor without anyone calling it borrowing. None of that requires fraud. It requires only that the people choosing the estimates are rewarded when the estimates are generous, and that nobody with authority insists on comparing reported profit with cash collected.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The signs were the gap between profit and cash. Reported profits were not turning into operating cash at the same rate. Amounts owed by customers for work done but not yet agreed grew. Debt rose while profits were reported. Suppliers were asked to wait longer for payment, in some cases being offered a financing arrangement through which they could be paid earlier at a discount. Each sign was visible in the published accounts or in the market. Read together, they said that the profit was an estimate the cash had not confirmed.

Step 6: Point of no return

Once the contract estimates were reassessed and written down, the reported equity and the lenders' confidence fell together, and the company needed new money just as its profit record lost credibility. Without fresh cash from lenders or government, there was no time to complete contracts and collect. The deeper point of no return came earlier, when large fixed-price contracts were taken on thin margins with optimistic assumptions that could not be unwound.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was reported profit built on estimates that cash did not confirm, in a structure where incentives rewarded the reported number and cash was consumed by dividends, pensions and debt while the contracts were still unfinished.

The pattern in small numbers

Hypothetical round numbers. Your contractor's monthly report on a $10,000,000 fixed-price contract claims 60 percent complete and a forecast margin of 8 percent, so $480,000 of profit earned to date. You reconcile. You have certified and paid $5,000,000. The contractor has paid its subcontractors and suppliers about $5,300,000. So on your job the contractor is $300,000 out of pocket while reporting $480,000 of profit. A month later it claims 70 percent, the forecast margin is unchanged, and its cash gap is $550,000. The gap widened two months running. Rule 18 says stop advancing money beyond verified work in place, ask for evidence of the cost to complete, and check whether subcontractors are being paid. A contractor that is funding your job from its own thin cash is one surprise away from walking off it.

What would have changed the outcome

Three controls, each cheap compared with the loss. A board that required every contract's reported margin to be shown beside the cash it had actually generated, so the gap was a standing agenda item rather than a footnote. A rule that profit depending on claims or variations not yet agreed is shown separately and excluded from any bonus or dividend decision until the money arrives. And a refusal to bid fixed-price contracts at thin margins where the cost risk could not be priced. None of these needs hindsight. Each would have forced the question "where is the cash?" years before the write-down.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is trusting the profit line because it comes from a large, respected company with audited accounts. Audits test accounts against standards; they do not guarantee that estimates of final outcomes will come true. The control is Rule 18: reconcile reported profit to cash every month, and watch the trend of the gap, not its size on one date.

The beginner's mistake

Paying ahead of work in place to help a contractor that says it is short of cash. It feels like partnership. In practice it turns you into the contractor's lender with none of a lender's protection. Help through faster certification of real work, not through advances.

Rule 18

Every month I reconcile the profit a project, partner or contractor reports to the cash actually collected and paid; if the gap widens two months running, I stop advancing money until the cash explains the profit.

Callback

In week 13, the Holyrood case taught that an early estimate quietly became the budget. Carillion is the accounting twin of that failure: an estimate of a contract's final outcome quietly became reported profit. In both, the cure is the same discipline: every estimate carries its class, its date and its basis, and nobody is allowed to forget that it is an estimate.

Recap

Carillion reported profit on long contracts using estimates of final outcomes, paid dividends and stretched suppliers while cash weakened, and collapsed when the estimates were written down. The root cause was profit unconfirmed by cash, with incentives rewarding the reported number. Rule 18 reconciles the two every month.

Next: Nadia, on profit and cash running on two clocks inside one development project.
checklist: Reconcile every contractor's reported progress to cash certified and cash paid.
Track the gap between reported profit and cash as a monthly trend.
Ask how much reported revenue depends on claims or variations not yet agreed.
Check that subcontractors and suppliers are being paid on time.
Never advance money ahead of verified work in place.
Read a contractor's accounts for growing receivables and rising debt.
Ask how management pay is linked to reported profit.
head: Field checklist
speak: Carillion was a large British construction and services contractor that went into liquidation in January 2018. It took on large fixed-price contracts at thin margins and reported profit as the work progressed, using estimates of each contract's final outcome, including claims not yet agreed. It kept paying dividends and funding a pension deficit while cash weakened, and it stretched payment terms to suppliers. In July 2017 it wrote down contract values, its credibility and its lenders' confidence fell together, and it ran out of time. The root cause was reported profit that cash never confirmed, in a structure where incentives rewarded the reported number. My rule: every month I reconcile reported profit to the cash actually collected and paid, for my own projects and for my contractors. If the gap widens two months running, I stop advancing money until the cash explains the profit.
terms: Percentage-of-completion accounting — recognising revenue and profit on a long contract as work progresses, based on estimated final results.
Profit warning — a company's announcement that its results will be materially worse than the market expects.
Supply chain finance — an arrangement where suppliers can be paid early at a discount by a financier while the buyer pays later.

hostile.q: Your contractor is a large, listed company with clean audited accounts. Why are you asking it for monthly cash reconciliations on my project?
hostile.a: Because an audit tests whether the accounts follow the standards, not whether the estimates of final contract outcomes will come true. On a fixed-price contract the contractor reports profit before it has the cash. I reconcile its claimed progress to what we have certified and what it has paid its subcontractors, every month. If that gap widens two months running, I stop advancing beyond verified work and ask for the cost to complete. It costs us an hour a month and it is the earliest warning we will get.

title: Two clocks on one project: profit, cash and the value of time
summary: A development project keeps two clocks: profit, which is recognised when work is earned or sold, and cash, which leaves early and returns late. Time value of money connects them, because a dollar of profit received later is worth less today. This checkpoint lesson draws the cash curve of one project and prices a year of delay in present value.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every project runs on two clocks. The profit clock says what you have earned; the cash clock says what you have in the bank. Time value of money is the gear that connects them, and it explains why a project with a positive profit can still destroy value.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what is Rule 18?

A. Every month I reconcile reported profit to cash actually collected and paid; if the gap widens two months running, I stop advancing money until the cash explains the profit.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what is lease-up?

A. The period after completion when a new building fills with tenants, during which income rises from near zero toward stabilised levels while costs continue.

Q. From the value week: what is a cap rate?

A. The yield buyers currently accept for a type of property: one year of stabilised net operating income divided by price.

Why this matters

Lenders fund the cash clock and investors judge the profit clock, and you answer to both. If you speak only in profit, a lender will ask how you pay the contractor in month 14. If you speak only in cash, an investor will ask whether the project is worth doing at all. The accounting weeks gave you the vocabulary; this checkpoint puts both clocks on one page.

The cash curve

Plain English: on a build-to-sell or build-and-refinance project, almost all the money goes out before any comes back.

The professional framing: cumulative project cash flow falls through land purchase and construction, reaches its lowest point, often called peak funding, around completion, and rises only as units sell or the building is refinanced or sold. Lenders usually require the equity to go in first, so the equity's own curve falls steeply at the start and stays flat until the end.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. The project from Sage's chain: total cost about $20,600,000, equity about $7,210,000 and a loan of about $13,390,000. In year one, land and early works consume the equity. In years one and two, the loan funds construction, and interest is capitalised: added to the loan and to project cost rather than paid from income, because there is no income yet. In year three the building is finished, leased and sold for about $23,000,000. The loan is repaid and the equity receives about $9,610,000.

On the profit clock, the accounts for a build-to-sell project typically show no profit in years one and two; the costs sit on the balance sheet as capitalised project cost, the work in progress from the owner accounting week, and profit of about $2,400,000 appears when the sale completes. On the cash clock, the equity is out $7,210,000 for most of three years. Same project, two very different pictures, and both are true.

Say that out loud now.

Peak funding is the number a lender cares about most. It tells them how much money must be in place before any comes back, and it sizes the interest reserve: the part of the loan set aside to pay interest while the building earns nothing. If lease-up runs three months late, the curve stays at its lowest point for three more months, the reserve runs down, and the gap must be filled with fresh equity. That is why the cash curve, not the profit figure, is the page a lender reads first.

Connecting the clocks: present value

Plain English: a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now, because money now could be earning something, and later carries risk.

The professional framing: net present value (NPV) discounts every future cash flow back to today at a rate that reflects what the equity could earn elsewhere at similar risk, then subtracts what was invested. A positive NPV means the project earns more than that rate; a negative NPV means it earns less, even if it shows a profit.

Worked example two. Suppose your equity requires 12 percent a year for this risk. The equity puts in $7,210,000 today and receives $9,610,000 in three years. Three years of discounting at 12 percent is a factor of 1.12 times 1.12 times 1.12, about 1.405. The present value of $9,610,000 is about $6,840,000. Less the $7,210,000 invested, the NPV is about negative $370,000.

Read that slowly. The project makes a $2,400,000 profit and still destroys about $370,000 of value for an investor who needs 12 percent. That matches the chain: the rough IRR was about 10 percent, below the 12 percent required. A positive profit is not the test. Beating your required rate is the test.

What a year of delay costs

Now delay the sale by one year, with the same profit. Four years of discounting is about 1.574. The present value of $9,610,000 becomes about $6,107,000 and the NPV about negative $1,103,000. One year of delay took roughly another $733,000 of value, before counting the extra interest, insurance, taxes and overhead that a real delay brings. In practice those carrying costs also eat the profit itself, so the true damage is larger. This is why schedule is a money topic and why the lender's monitor watches it.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: your personal balance sheet has the same two clocks. An investment can show a gain on paper while tying up cash you may need. Before you commit equity to a three-year project, check that your liquidity floor still holds with that equity locked away for four years, not three, because delays arrive more often than early finishes. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal decision.

Monthly thread: time and energy on a rotating shift

A checkpoint week asks for recall under pressure, and recall depends heavily on sleep. On a rotating schedule, plan the hard work, the mock interview and the recording, for the first or second day after your sleep has realigned, not the first night shift or the day after a run of nights. Use the low-energy days for reading and listening, and the clear days for performing.

Keep the study block short and fixed, at the same point in your waking day rather than the same clock time, because your body clock moves with the roster. Record the score and the shift beside it in your journal. After a few checkpoints you will see your own pattern, and you can schedule real meetings by it. If fatigue is persistent, check that with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving a project on profit alone. Profit ignores time, so a slow project and a fast one with the same profit look identical, and a project below your required rate can still look like a success. The control is to show three lines on every approval: profit, IRR against your required rate, and NPV at that rate, with a one-year-delay case beside it.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing a discount rate after seeing the answer. If you pick 8 percent because 12 percent makes the NPV negative, you have not measured the project; you have hidden it. Write your required rate down before you model, base it on what similar-risk investments earn, and keep it the same across every deal you compare.

Callback

In the physiology week you learned that a tired mind defaults to the easy, familiar answer. On a project, the easy answer is profit, because it is one number and it is usually positive. The harder answers, cash timing and present value, are the ones most likely to be skipped after a long shift. Put them on the template so tiredness cannot leave them out.

Recap

Profit and cash are two clocks. The cash curve falls through construction and rises only at sale or refinance, and interest is capitalised along the way. Present value connects the clocks: a profitable project can still have a negative NPV, and a year of delay can cost several hundred thousand dollars of value before any extra cost.

Next: LEX, on why every number you hand to a lender or investor is a promise of some kind.
checklist: Draw the cumulative cash curve and mark peak funding.
Show when profit is recognised in the accounts, separately from cash.
Write your required rate of return before you model.
Show profit, IRR against the required rate, and NPV on every approval.
Run a one-year-delay case and price it in present value.
Check that your liquidity floor holds with equity locked up for an extra year.
Schedule hard performance tasks for clear days in your shift rotation.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every project runs on two clocks. The profit clock usually shows nothing until the sale, because costs are capitalised as work in progress. The cash clock shows equity going out first, the loan funding construction with interest capitalised, and the money coming back only at completion and sale. Present value connects them. On a hypothetical project, equity of 7.21 million returns 9.61 million in three years: a 2.4 million profit. At a required 12 percent, the present value of that return is about 6.84 million, so the NPV is about negative 370,000. The project is profitable and still below my required rate. Delay it one year and the NPV falls to about negative 1.1 million, before extra carrying costs. So every approval shows profit, IRR against my required rate, and NPV, with a delay case beside it, and I set the required rate before I model.
terms: Peak funding — the point where a project's cumulative cash outflow is largest, usually near completion.
Net present value — future cash flows discounted to today at a required rate, minus the amount invested.
Discount rate — the annual return used to convert future money into today's value, reflecting what similar-risk investments earn.

hostile.q: The project makes 2.4 million of profit. Why are you telling the committee it destroys value?
hostile.a: Because our equity is out for three years and requires 12 percent. Discounted at 12 percent, the 9.61 million we get back is worth about 6.84 million today, against 7.21 million invested, so the NPV is about negative 370,000. The project's rough IRR is about 10 percent. It is profitable, but it pays us less than we can earn elsewhere at this risk. At a lower land price the NPV turns positive, and that is the price I will offer.

title: Every number you hand over is a promise of some kind
summary: The money phase produced numbers: budgets, rents, values, returns and cash forecasts. Once those numbers go to a lender, investor or buyer, the law treats them as statements of fact, forecasts or opinions, each with different consequences. This checkpoint lesson sorts them, shows how a certified number can trigger a default, and gives a labelling habit that protects you.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a number on your screen is analysis; the same number in a lender's file is a statement you made. The law asks what kind of statement it was, a fact, a forecast or an opinion, and who was entitled to rely on it. Get the label right and most of the legal risk in the money phase falls away.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: why can a profitable project have a negative net present value?

A. Because profit ignores time. If the return, discounted at the investor's required rate, is worth less today than the equity invested, the project earns less than that rate even though it shows a profit.

Q. From the valuation week: what are the intended user and the effective date of an appraisal?

A. The intended user is the party the appraisal was written for and who may rely on it. The effective date is the date the opinion of value applies to. Outside either, the opinion may not support a decision.

Q. From the first pro forma week: what four things should travel with every estimate?

A. Its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency.

Why this matters

Lenders lend and investors invest on your numbers. If a number turns out wrong, the first question is not whether you were careless but what you said: did you state a fact, make a forecast, or give an opinion, and did you say what it was based on? Those distinctions decide whether a wrong number is an honest miss or something the other side can sue on, rescind a deal over, or call a default for. Concepts only here; the rules differ by jurisdiction, so verify against the primary source before you rely on them.

Fact, forecast, opinion

Plain English first. A fact is something that is true or false now: "the site is 2,000 square metres." A forecast is about the future: "we expect rents of $30 a square metre a month." An opinion is a judgement: "in my view the market cap rate is about 5 percent."

The professional framing. In many common-law systems, a false statement of fact that induces someone to contract can give them a remedy for misrepresentation, which may include damages or setting the contract aside. A forecast or opinion is generally treated more leniently, because everyone knows the future is uncertain, but it is not free. A forecast can carry an implied statement that you honestly hold it and have reasonable grounds for it. If you had no reasonable basis, or knew facts that undermined it, the forecast can become actionable. Separately, statements to investors may be governed by securities rules that impose stricter standards; that is a later phase.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Your investor memo says: "Rents of $31 per square metre are achievable." You based it on asking rents in listings, and you had a rent survey showing signed rents of $30, which you left out. That is the dangerous version: it reads as a fact, and you held information that undermined it. The safer version: "We assume rents of $31 per square metre, about 3 percent above signed rents of $30 in the four newest comparable buildings surveyed on a stated date. Each $1 change moves the land value by about $666,000." Same number, now labelled as an assumption with its basis and its sensitivity.

Say that out loud now.

Reliance: who may use your number

A statement creates risk only toward those who can rely on it. That is why appraisals name an intended user, why consultants' reports often say they may be relied on only by the client, and why lenders ask for reliance letters from your appraiser, engineer and cost consultant. When you pass a consultant's report to an investor, you may be repeating the consultant's statement as your own, without the consultant standing behind it for that investor. Say so: "Attached is the cost consultant's report prepared for us. It has not been addressed to you, and you should not rely on it without the consultant's agreement."

Certified numbers: where a promise becomes a default

Some numbers are not just statements; they are certifications under a contract. A construction loan agreement commonly requires the borrower to certify, with each draw, that the remaining loan plus equity still covers the cost to complete. Lenders usually call this being in balance. If the certificate is wrong, it can be an event of default, which may let the lender stop funding or demand repayment, even if the error was honest.

Worked example two, hypothetical. You certify a cost to complete of $4,000,000 with $4,100,000 of undrawn loan and equity remaining, so the loan appears in balance by $100,000. Your contractor's own latest estimate, sitting in your inbox, says $4,600,000. The true position is out of balance by $500,000. Under a typical agreement you would have to fund that gap with equity before the next draw, and the inaccurate certificate itself may be a default. If you had certified $4,600,000, you would have faced the same $500,000 call, but without the default. The gap was going to cost money either way; the false certificate added a legal problem to a financial one.

Which frameworks are rules and which are practice

The phase used three kinds of guide, and they carry different weight. Financial statements are prepared under an accounting framework, a recognised set of standards for when revenue, profit and cost are recorded; when you say your accounts follow one, you are stating a fact that can be checked. Appraisals are prepared under professional valuation standards that govern definitions such as market value, intended use and assumptions; an appraiser who departs from them must say so. Estimate classes, contingency percentages, loan-to-cost limits and profit-on-cost targets are different again: they are commercial practice, not law or standards. Quote them as practice: "a typical working figure in this market," never "the required figure." Calling a practice a rule is itself a misstatement.

A labelling habit

Every number that leaves your hands carries four tags: what it is (fact, assumption or opinion), its source, its date and its sensitivity or range. This is the estimate discipline from the first pro forma week, extended to every number. It costs a column in a spreadsheet and a sentence in a memo. It turns most future disputes into a question of whether the assumption was reasonable at the time, which is the question you want to be asked.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where you operate, before any investor memo, offering document or lender certificate goes out.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the confident sentence: a forecast written as a fact, because it reads better. "Rents are $31" sells; "we assume $31, based on this, with this sensitivity" protects. The control is the four-tag rule, enforced by a review in which someone other than the author reads every number in the document and asks, "Fact, assumption or opinion, and where is the basis?"

The beginner's mistake

Believing a disclaimer at the bottom of the page cures a misleading sentence at the top. General disclaimers can help, but in many systems they do not protect a statement you knew, or should have known, was unsupported. Fix the sentence, not the footnote.

Callback

In week 2 you met inversion: ask how a plan could fail, and design against that. Apply it to every number you send: "If this number turns out wrong, what will the reader say I told them?" If the honest answer is "that it was a fact," and it was only your hope, rewrite it before it leaves.

Recap

Numbers you hand over are facts, forecasts or opinions, and each carries a different risk. A forecast needs an honest belief and a reasonable basis. Reliance decides who can hold you to a number, and a certified number under a loan can become a default. Tag every number with type, source, date and sensitivity.

Next: Sage, working backward from a target return through the whole chain to the most you can pay for land.
checklist: Tag every number with type: fact, assumption or opinion.
Add the source, date and sensitivity to every assumption.
Never leave out information you hold that undermines a forecast.
State who may rely on any report you pass on.
Reconcile every draw certificate to the contractor's latest estimate.
Have someone other than the author check every number before release.
Get a lawyer's review before any memo, offering document or certificate goes out.
head: Field checklist
speak: Once a number leaves my hands it is a statement, and the law asks what kind. A fact is true or false now. A forecast is about the future and generally carries an implied promise that I honestly hold it and have reasonable grounds. An opinion is a judgement. A false fact that induces a contract can support a claim for misrepresentation, and a forecast with no reasonable basis can too. Reliance decides who can hold me to it, which is why appraisals name an intended user. Under a construction loan, some numbers are certifications: if I certify the loan is in balance when my contractor's estimate says otherwise, that can be a default on top of the money gap. So I tag every number with its type, source, date and sensitivity, and I have someone else check every number before it goes out.
terms: Misrepresentation — a false statement of fact that induces another party to enter a contract, which may give them a remedy.
Reliance letter — a letter from a consultant permitting a named third party, such as a lender, to rely on its report.
In balance — the loan test that remaining loan and equity cover the full remaining cost to complete.

hostile.q: Your memo said rents of 31 dollars were achievable. They came in at 29. Why shouldn't the investors treat that as a misstatement?
hostile.a: Because the memo did not say they were achievable; it said we assumed 31, about 3 percent above signed rents of 30 in four named buildings surveyed on a stated date, and it showed the effect of each dollar on value. The assumption was reasonable on that evidence and the sensitivity was disclosed. The miss is real and we will report its effect on returns this quarter, with what we are doing about lease-up.

title: Backward through the whole chain: from target return to maximum land price
summary: This checkpoint calculation starts from a finished outcome, the equity multiple an investor needs, and works backward through sale proceeds, debt and total cost to the most the land can cost. It then repeats the exercise after a hypothetical tax leakage and at a worse exit cap rate, showing how far each lens moves the maximum price.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most useful calculation in this phase runs backward. Start from the return your equity must earn, walk back through the sale, the loan and the costs, and the last number standing is the most you can pay for land. Then change one lens at a time and watch that number move.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what four tags travel with every number you hand over?

A. Its type, meaning fact, assumption or opinion; its source; its date; and its sensitivity or range.

Q. From the valuation week: what NOI does a $20,000,000 value at a 5.75 percent cap rate imply?

A. Value times cap rate, about $1,150,000 a year.

Q. From the value week: what is the development spread?

A. Yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin you are paid for taking development risk.

Why this matters

Forward models start from the land price and tell you the return. That invites you to accept the seller's price and hope the return is good enough. Working backward fixes the return first, because it is the thing your investors actually require, and lets the land price be whatever is left. It is the residual method extended to the equity, and it is how you decide what to offer before anyone names a price.

The finished outcome we start from

A different hypothetical project from this week's chain: 100 apartments. The investors require an equity multiple of 1.6 over about 3 years, which is roughly a 17 percent internal rate of return. The lender will provide 65 percent of total cost, a commercial practice in this hypothetical market, not a rule. All figures are hypothetical round numbers.

Step 1: The sale proceeds

Stabilised net operating income is forecast at $1,600,000 a year. At a 5 percent cap rate, value is $1,600,000 divided by 0.05, which is $32,000,000. Selling costs of 2 percent take $640,000. Net sale proceeds are $31,360,000.

Step 2: What the equity gets back, as a formula

Call total cost C. The loan is 0.65 C and the equity is 0.35 C. At the sale, the loan is repaid, so the equity receives $31,360,000 minus 0.65 C. The investors need that to be 1.6 times their equity, which is 1.6 times 0.35 C, or 0.56 C.

Step 3: Solve for total cost

Set the two equal: $31,360,000 minus 0.65 C equals 0.56 C. Move the C terms together: $31,360,000 equals 1.21 C. Divide: C equals about $25,917,000. That is the most the whole project can cost and still give the equity 1.6 times its money.

Step 4: Subtract every cost except land

Hard costs are $18,000,000. Soft costs at 18 percent are $3,240,000. Finance costs are estimated at $1,500,000; in a full model they depend on the land price too, but we hold them fixed here for clarity. Non-land cost is $22,740,000. The maximum land price is $25,917,000 less $22,740,000, about $3,177,000. Call it $3,180,000, or about $31,800 per apartment.

Step 5: Check it forward

Always check a backward answer by running it forward. Equity is 35 percent of $25,917,000, about $9,071,000. The loan is about $16,846,000. The equity receives $31,360,000 less $16,846,000, about $14,514,000. Divide by $9,071,000: 1.60. The arithmetic holds. Yield on cost is $1,600,000 divided by $25,917,000, about 6.2 percent, a spread of about 120 basis points over the 5 percent cap rate.

Say that out loud now.

Step 6: Add the tax lens

The returns week warned that investors spend after-tax money. Suppose, purely as a hypothetical illustration and not a rate anyone should use, that taxes at the entity and personal level take 25 percent of the profit. For the investors to receive 1.6 times after tax, the after-tax profit must be 0.6 times equity, so the pre-tax profit must be 0.6 divided by 0.75, which is 0.8 times equity. The pre-tax multiple needed is 1.8.

Repeat Step 3 with 1.8: the equity needs 1.8 times 0.35 C, which is 0.63 C. So $31,360,000 equals 0.65 C plus 0.63 C, which is 1.28 C. C is $24,500,000. Less $22,740,000 of non-land cost, the maximum land price is $1,760,000. The tax lens alone took about $1,420,000, roughly 45 percent, off what you can pay. The real tax position depends on the structure, the jurisdictions and the people involved; a qualified tax adviser must work it out before you rely on any figure.

Step 7: Add the exit cap rate lens

Now return to the pre-tax case and ask what happens if the exit cap rate is 5.5 percent instead of 5. Value becomes $1,600,000 divided by 0.055, about $29,091,000, and after 2 percent selling costs about $28,509,000. If you had paid $3,180,000 for land, total cost is still $25,917,000, the loan $16,846,000, and the equity gets back about $11,663,000. The multiple falls to about 1.29, roughly a 9 percent rough IRR. Half a point of cap rate cut the investors' gain from 60 percent to about 29 percent.

Reverse it once more. For 1.6 times at a 5.5 percent exit, C must be $28,509,000 divided by 1.21, about $23,561,000, and the land can cost only about $821,000. The price that works at a 5 percent exit is almost four times the price that works at 5.5 percent.

Step 8: The smell test against the market

Convert each ceiling into the unit the market uses. The pre-tax ceiling is about $31,800 per apartment, the after-tax ceiling about $17,600 and the stress ceiling about $8,200. Now compare with recent land sales nearby, reversed the way last week taught. Suppose they cluster around $25,000 per buildable apartment. That tells you something important: other buyers are paying above your after-tax ceiling. Either they have a lower tax cost, a lower required return, cheaper construction, or higher rents than you assume, or they are accepting less than you would. Find out which before you either raise your price to match them or dismiss them as reckless. A gap between your ceiling and the market is a question, not an answer.

Reading the three answers together

You now have three maximum land prices from one building: about $3,180,000 pre-tax at a 5 percent exit, about $1,760,000 after the hypothetical tax, and about $821,000 if the exit cap rate moves half a point. A disciplined offer is not the highest of these. It is a price at which the deal still works in the case you think is likely and survives in the case you fear. The backward method is how you see that case before you are committed to it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is solving backward from your target and then treating the answer as the price you should pay. The backward answer is the ceiling at which the deal exactly meets the target, with no cushion. The control is to set your offer below the ceiling of your stress case, not your base case, and to write both ceilings in the investment memo.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting that finance costs depend on the land price and on time. A cheaper site lowers the loan and the interest; a slower lease-up raises the interest. Hold them fixed for a first pass, as we did, but rerun the full model before you sign anything.

Callback

In the second pro forma week Sage reversed a required value into the rent it demands. Today you reversed a required return into the land it allows. The method is the same staircase, one step longer: return to equity, equity to cost, cost to land. Every price in development can be read this way, and every one should be.

Recap

Fix the return first. Sale proceeds less the loan must equal the required multiple of equity; solve for total cost, subtract non-land costs, and the land is what remains. Check it forward. Then add the tax lens and the exit cap rate lens and offer below the ceiling of your stress case.

Next: Roman runs a full mock investment committee on this phase.
checklist: Write the required equity multiple or IRR before you model.
Compute net sale proceeds after selling costs.
Express equity returned as net proceeds minus the loan, and solve for total cost.
Subtract every non-land cost to find the maximum land price.
Check every backward answer by running it forward.
Repeat with the after-tax target, using figures from a tax adviser.
Repeat at an exit cap rate half a point worse and offer below the stress-case ceiling.
head: Field checklist
speak: I work backward from the return. Say investors need 1.6 times their equity in three years and the lender gives 65 percent of cost. The finished building earns 1.6 million, so at a 5 percent cap rate it is worth 32 million, about 31.36 million after selling costs. The equity gets back proceeds minus the loan: 31.36 million minus 0.65 times cost must equal 0.56 times cost. So total cost can be about 25.9 million, and after 22.74 million of non-land cost, the land can cost about 3.18 million. I check it forward and it holds. Then I add lenses. If a hypothetical 25 percent of profit leaks to tax, the land ceiling falls to about 1.76 million. If the exit cap rate is 5.5 percent, it falls to about 821,000. So I offer below the ceiling of my stress case, never at the base-case ceiling.
terms: Equity multiple — total cash returned to the equity divided by the equity invested.
Ceiling price — the highest price at which a deal exactly meets its required return, with no cushion.
Stress case — a version of the model with one or more adverse assumptions, used to test whether the deal survives.

hostile.q: Your model says this land is worth 3.18 million to us. Why are you only offering 1.5 million?
hostile.a: Because 3.18 million is the ceiling at which we exactly hit our target, pre-tax, at a 5 percent exit, with no cushion. After tax the ceiling is about 1.76 million on our hypothetical leakage, and at a 5.5 percent exit it is about 821,000. An offer of 1.5 million keeps the after-tax target in our base case, and even at a 5.5 percent exit our multiple stays near 1.5 instead of falling to about 1.3. If the seller shows evidence that lifts NOI, I will rerun all three.

title: Mock investment committee: the whole money phase in one meeting
summary: A full mock meeting with a credit officer and an equity partner, built on one hypothetical 100-apartment project. Each question tests a link of the money chain: spread, valuation, estimate class, cash timing, returns and tax. Model answers, the question behind each question, the lines never to say and how to hold your state are all scripted.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an investment committee is not asking whether your spreadsheet is right. It is asking whether you have tried to break your own deal and can say, in numbers, what would make you stop. This mock meeting runs the whole money phase in about twenty minutes.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what is a ceiling price?

A. The highest price at which a deal exactly meets its required return, with no cushion. Offer below the ceiling of your stress case, not your base case.

Q. From the valuation week: what does a lender do when the appraisal comes in low?

A. Sizes the loan on the lower value if that test binds, which raises the equity you must contribute. You respond with evidence through the lender, never by pressuring the appraiser.

Q. From the communication weeks: what does "bottom line first" mean in a meeting?

A. Open with your recommendation and the one reason that matters most, then give the support. The listener should know your answer in the first thirty seconds.

Why this matters

Every phase ends in a room where someone else decides whether your numbers deserve their money. The skills from the communication weeks only work if the money is solid underneath them, and the money only gets heard if it is delivered in order. This rehearsal puts both together. Run it aloud, standing, with a timer.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. You are asking for equity and a construction loan for a 100-apartment building. Forecast NOI is $1,600,000, value at a 5 percent cap rate $32,000,000, non-land cost $22,740,000. You have agreed land at $1,500,000, so total cost is $24,240,000. Around the table: Tom, a credit officer from the lender, careful and literal; and Ruth, an equity partner who lost money on a project that ran a year late. You have five minutes to present.

Your opening

Say: "I'm asking for $8,500,000 of equity and a $15,750,000 construction loan for a 100-unit rental building. The bottom line: at today's signed rents and a 5 percent exit cap rate it returns about 1.8 times equity before tax over three years. More important, it still returns about 1.5 times if the exit cap rate is 5.5 percent. The land is agreed at $1,500,000, well below the $3,180,000 ceiling, and that gap is our cushion. Here are the three things that would make me stop."

Then name them: rents below $29 a square metre in the next survey; a contractor's price more than 5 percent above the estimate; or a planning condition that cuts more than 5 units.

Say that out loud now.

The questions, and the question behind each

Tom: "What's your yield on cost and spread?" Behind it: is the margin real, or is the return coming from leverage? Answer: "Yield on cost is $1,600,000 over $24,240,000, about 6.6 percent. The spread over a 5 percent cap rate is about 160 basis points. That is the number I'd ask you to judge the deal on, not the IRR."

Tom: "Where does the 5 percent cap rate come from?" Behind it: are you using an opinion as a fact? Answer: "From four sales of new apartment buildings in the last eighteen months, reversed to implied cap rates between 4.8 and 5.3 percent. I've used 5 for the base and 5.5 for the stress case, and both are in the memo with their sources."

Ruth: "How firm is the $18,000,000 hard cost?" Behind it: am I about to be called for more money? Answer: "It's a class 3 estimate from our quantity surveyor, in the industry's common classification, prepared from a developed design with a stated accuracy range, plus 8 percent contingency. Estimate classes and contingency percentages are industry practice, not rules. If tenders come in 5 percent high, the deal still clears 1.6 times, and I won't sign a construction contract above that."

Ruth: "What happens if it runs a year late?" Behind it: will this be my last project again? Answer: "A year's delay costs about $1,200,000 in extra interest and carrying costs on our numbers, and the present value of your return falls further on top of that. The interest reserve covers six extra months; beyond that we would call equity. I'm asking for a contingent equity commitment of $1,000,000 now, so a delay is a known cost, not a crisis."

Tom: "Are you certifying the loan in balance on this budget?" Behind it: will your draw certificates be honest? Answer: "Every draw certificate will be reconciled to the contractor's latest cost-to-complete, and I'll send you that reconciliation with each draw. If the two disagree, I'll certify on the higher number."

Ruth: "What do I actually take home after tax?" Behind it: are you quoting a number I'll never see? Answer: "The 1.8 times is before tax. Our tax adviser's preliminary view is in appendix C, and on that view the after-tax multiple is materially lower. I'd rather you judge the deal after tax, and that's why the land price is set where it is."

The lines never to say

Never say "The IRR is 22 percent" as your opening, because it leads with the most derived number and invites the committee to find what it hides. Never say "Costs are locked" when you hold an estimate, not a contract. Never say "Cap rates won't move." Never say "The appraisal will come in at 32," because you do not control the appraiser. And never answer a question you have not understood; ask Tom to repeat it.

When to stay silent

After you name the three things that would make you stop, stop talking. Let the committee absorb that you have a walk-away. After Ruth asks about delay, wait a beat before answering; the pause tells her you are taking her history seriously. And when Tom is reading your appendix, do not narrate it. Silence while someone reads is respect, not awkwardness.

Holding your state

Ruth may say, sharply, "I've heard every one of these promises before." Do not defend yourself. Acknowledge, bridge, answer: "You have, and some of them were broken. That's why the contingent equity and the stop conditions are in writing, not in my presentation." Keep your hands still and your voice low at the end of each sentence. Before you walk in, breathe out slowly a few times while seated, a practitioner habit with research support. If your mind blanks, say "Let me give you the number rather than a guess," and look it up in your one-page summary.

Closing the meeting

Say: "To summarise: a 160 basis point spread, a deal that survives a half-point move in the exit cap rate, a cost cushion against a 5 percent overrun, contingent equity for a delay, and three written stop conditions. What would you need to see to approve it?" Then write down exactly what they say and confirm it in an email the same day.

Scoring the mock

Play it once alone, then once with someone reading Tom and Ruth. Score yourself 1 to 5 on four measures: did you lead with the spread rather than the IRR; did every answer contain a number; did you name your stop conditions without being asked; and did you stay calm when Ruth pushed. A 3 on the last measure is normal the first time.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defending every assumption as if conceding one would sink the deal. Committees trust a presenter who concedes the weak points and shows what protects against them. The control is to bring the weaknesses yourself: the stress case, the delay cost and the after-tax figure, before anyone asks.

The beginner's mistake

Answering the question asked instead of the question behind it. Ruth's question about delay is really about whether she will be called for money without warning. Answer that fear directly, with the contingent equity, and the literal question answers itself.

Callback

Two weeks ago, in the low-appraisal meeting, Roman taught that you bring evidence through the lender rather than pressure on the appraiser. The same principle runs through this whole room: every answer is evidence plus a control, never persuasion alone. That is what a lender means by a sponsor they can work with.

Recap

Open with the request and the bottom line, lead with the spread, name your stop conditions, and answer the question behind each question with a number and a control. Concede weak points before you are asked. Close by asking what they need to approve, and confirm it in writing.

Next: Kema's checkpoint for the money phase, with a mock interview, a recording and the rules so far.
checklist: Open with the request, the bottom line and the stress-case result.
Lead with yield on cost and spread, not the IRR.
Name three written stop conditions without being asked.
Give the source and range behind the cap rate.
State the estimate class and contingency behind the hard cost.
Price a one-year delay and propose how it is funded.
Close by asking what they need to approve, and confirm it in writing the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: In an investment committee I open with the request and the bottom line: 8.5 million of equity and a 15.75 million loan for a 100-unit building, returning about 1.8 times before tax, and still about 1.5 times if the exit cap rate rises to 5.5 percent. Then I lead with the spread: about 6.6 percent yield on cost, 160 basis points over the cap rate. I give the cap rate's source and range, the hard cost's estimate class and contingency, the cost of a year's delay and how it is funded, and the after-tax position from our adviser. I name three stop conditions without being asked. I never lead with the IRR, never say costs are locked when they are estimated, and never predict the appraisal. When the partner pushes, I acknowledge, bridge and answer with a control. I close by asking what they need to approve, and I confirm it in writing.
terms: Investment committee — the group inside a lender or investor that approves or rejects a funding request.
Contingent equity — equity committed in advance to be called only if a stated event, such as delay or overrun, occurs.
Stop condition — a written, measurable event that would make the sponsor halt or abandon the project.

hostile.q: Every sponsor tells me their deal survives the stress case. Why should I believe yours?
hostile.a: Because the stress case is written into the deal, not just the model. Land is agreed at 1.5 million against a 3.18 million base-case ceiling, so a half-point cap rate move still leaves about 1.5 times. There is a 1 million contingent equity commitment for delay, a cost cushion against a 5 percent overrun, and three stop conditions in the memo that I will not cross. You can hold me to each of them in the loan documents.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: the language of money
summary: The checkpoint for the money phase: a six-question mock interview covering value, statements, accounting, the pro forma, returns, valuation and reverse engineering, then a three-minute recorded explanation scored for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. It ends with every rule so far, read aloud and restated.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a phase is learned when you can explain it under pressure, out loud, in three minutes, without notes. Today you test that for the language of money, and you write the score down so the next checkpoint has something to beat.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what should you lead with in an investment committee, the IRR or the spread?

A. The spread. Yield on cost against the market cap rate shows whether the margin is real; the IRR is the most derived number on the page and can be mostly leverage.

Q. From the second pro forma week: why does a small rent error grow by the time it reaches land value?

A. Because rent flows down the staircase into NOI, NOI is divided by a small cap rate to give value, and land is the residual that absorbs the whole change.

Q. From the first checkpoint: what four measures do you score a recording on?

A. Accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question.

Why this matters

Every phase after this one speaks the language of money: law and tax change after-tax returns, approvals change value, debt changes leverage, construction changes cost and time. If the vocabulary of this phase is shaky, every later lesson rests on sand. A checkpoint is also the only place in the course where you produce evidence of your own progress: a recording and a score you can compare with the next one.

The mock interview

Read each question, answer it aloud before reading the model answer, then compare. Be strict.

Question 1. A partner says the deal returns a 20 percent IRR. What two numbers do you ask for first, and why?

Answer: The yield on cost against the market cap rate, which is the development spread, and the equity multiple. The spread shows whether the margin is real or the return is mostly leverage; the multiple shows how much wealth is created, not just how fast. Worked check: a 60 basis point spread can still show a 10 percent IRR on 65 percent debt, and half a point of exit cap rate can wipe out most of the profit.

Question 2. The project shows a profit but the lender is worried. What are they worried about?

Answer: Cash timing. Profit is recognised at the sale or as work is earned, while equity and loan go out first and interest is capitalised. The lender cares about peak funding, the interest reserve and whether the loan stays in balance. A profitable project can still run out of money in month 14.

Question 3. Explain net present value in one breath, and say why a profitable project can have a negative one.

Answer: Net present value discounts future cash back to today at the return the money requires and subtracts what was invested. If the project earns less than that rate, its NPV is negative even with a profit. Worked check: $7,210,000 returning $9,610,000 in three years at 12 percent has an NPV of about negative $370,000.

Question 4. Your hard cost is an early estimate. How do you present it?

Answer: With its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency, stated as a range rather than a single figure, and labelled as an estimate, never as a fixed price. Classes and contingency percentages are industry practice, not rules.

Question 5. An appraisal shows $15,000,000 as-complete. What do you check before relying on it?

Answer: The intended user, the effective date, the evidence behind the cap rate, the direction and size of the adjustments, any extraordinary assumption such as a rezoning, and the as-is value beside the conditional one. Professional sign-off required: a licensed or designated appraiser.

Question 6. Investors need 1.6 times their equity, the lender gives 65 percent of cost, and net sale proceeds are $31,360,000. What is the most the project can cost?

Answer: Proceeds minus 0.65 C must equal 1.6 times 0.35 C, so $31,360,000 equals 1.21 C, and C is about $25,917,000. Subtract every non-land cost to find the land ceiling, then offer below the ceiling of the stress case.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Open the voice recorder on your phone and record a three-minute explanation of this phase, as if to a new equity partner who has never developed. Use this structure: the money chain, from rent to NOI to value to margin to return to cash and tax; the one link most likely to break and why; how you reverse engineer any price you are shown; and one failure case with its prevention rule. No notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions and numbers right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip, such as calling cap rate price divided by income.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow the chain in order? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds like someone who has done this many times.
  4. The hard question. Did you name the weakest link and what would make you walk away, unprompted? A 5 raises the hard point before the listener can.

Write the four scores, the date and the shift you were on in your decision journal. An example of honest scoring: if you explained NOI correctly but forgot that it excludes debt payments, accuracy is a 4. If you opened with the IRR rather than the chain, structure is a 3, however good the rest was.

What to do with the scores

Take your lowest score and work on that one alone this week. If accuracy was lowest, reread the lesson where the error came from and rebuild the definition in your own words. If structure was lowest, write the five links on a card and record again using only the card. If composure was lowest, record again at a deliberately slower pace and count filler words on playback. If the hard question was lowest, practise opening with the risk: "The link that breaks this deal is..." Record once more at the end of the week and compare. Keep both recordings; the difference between them is your evidence.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from. Pay particular attention to Rules 10, 13, 14, 16, 17 and 18, the money phase's rules, and notice how many of them say the same thing from different angles: price what exists, label what is assumed, and let cash confirm profit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading what you meant rather than what you said. The control is the recording, which does not care what you meant. Score the tape, not the intention, and if a friend or mentor will listen, ask them to score it too and compare.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the model answers instead of answering aloud first. Reading gives the feeling of mastery without the evidence. The discomfort of hearing yourself explain cap rates and present value is the training effect; it is what makes the real committee feel familiar.

Callback

In week 6 you practised presenting numbers aloud: round them, give the unit, and say what they mean before the next one. Listen for that on your recording. "Twenty-three million of value, which is a 60 basis point spread, which is thin" is three numbers a listener can follow. "Twenty-two million nine hundred and eighty-two thousand" is one they cannot.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud before reading the answers. Record three minutes on the phase without notes, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores and your shift in the journal. Then read every rule aloud and restate it.

Next: LEX opens the law and tax phase with where law comes from: sources, systems, courts and precedent.
checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: This phase is one chain. Rent less vacancy and expenses is net operating income. NOI divided by the cap rate is value. Value against total cost gives yield on cost and the development spread, which is the margin I am paid for risk. Leverage turns that margin into a return, which I read as both an IRR and an equity multiple, and timing and tax decide how much reaches me as cash. Profit and cash run on different clocks, so a profitable project can still run out of money or have a negative net present value. The links that break most often are the exit cap rate, the estimate class behind the cost, and cash timing. I reverse engineer every price into what must be true, and I work backward from the return I need to the most I can pay for land. My rules: price what exists, label what is assumed, and let cash confirm profit.
terms: Development spread — yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin paid for development risk.
Net present value — future cash flows discounted at the required rate, minus the amount invested.
Equity multiple — total cash returned to the equity divided by the equity invested.

hostile.q: You have shown me profit, IRR and a multiple. Which number would you stake your own money on, and why?
hostile.a: None of them alone. I would stake it on the spread and the stress case together: yield on cost against the market cap rate, and whether the deal still returns my required multiple with the exit cap rate half a point worse. Profit ignores time, IRR can be mostly leverage, and the multiple ignores speed. If the spread is wide enough to survive the stress case, the other three numbers are worth reading.
